narrative:
The model predicted a 77% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure. Both rankings placed you at the very bottom decile (1 out of 10), far below the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.10 was the third most influential piece of information. Unlike the two rankings, this actually worked in your favor by slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure, yet it was not enough to offset the impact of your class standings.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude that the likelihood of passing the bar on the first try was too low for admission. Gender, race, family income bracket, LSAT score, and planned full-time status played no role in the protected attributes and were not among the top drivers.

You should focus on strengthening your academic trajectory. Retaking courses to raise your GPA, seeking intensive bar-preparation support, or gaining additional legal experience before reapplying could improve your profile for future cycles. Consider speaking with an admissions counselor about specific steps that have helped similar applicants.
